title: Sequentially Ordinal Rank Tracker
statement:
Each scenic location has a `name`, which no other location shares, and an integer `score`. One location ranks above another when its score is higher; when the scores are equal, the location whose name comes first lexicographically ranks higher.

Design the class `SORTracker`, which starts with no locations:

- `SORTracker()` creates an empty tracker.
- `add(name, score)` stores a new location.
- `get()` returns the name of the `i`-th best location among all locations stored so far, where `i` is how many times `get` has been called, counting this call. So the first call returns the best location, the second call the second best at that moment, and so on.

The calls are guaranteed to never ask `get` for more locations than have been added at that point.
constraints: name consists of lowercase English letters
every name is unique among all locations
At any time, the number of calls to get does not exceed the number of calls to add
At most 4 * 10^4 calls in total are made to add and get
notes:
## Intuition

Sorting every location on each `get` works but costs O(n log n) per query. Notice that the query index only grows: after `k` calls to `get`, the next call wants the `(k + 1)`-th best. So split the locations in two groups: the `k` best ones, and everything else. The answer to the next query is simply the best location of the second group. Two heaps keep both groups cheap to maintain, like the classic running-median trick.

## Approach

1. `better(a, b)` says whether `a` ranks above `b`: higher score, or equal score and smaller name.
2. `top` holds the `k` best locations with the **worst** of them at its root; `rest` holds all other locations with the **best** of them at its root. Every location in `top` ranks above every location in `rest`.
3. `add`: push the new location into `top`, then pop the worst of `top` and push it into `rest`. `top` keeps its size `k` and still holds the `k` best.
4. `get`: pop the best location of `rest`; it is exactly the `(k + 1)`-th best overall. Push it into `top` (now of size `k + 1`) and return its name.
5. `push` and `pop` are a plain binary heap whose order is given by the heap's `first` function.

## Example 1, step by step

Adding `bradford 2` and `branford 3` sends both through the empty `top` into `rest`. The first `get` pops `branford` (score 3) from `rest` into `top`. Adding `alps 2` enters `top`, but the worst of `{branford, alps}` is `alps`, so it moves to `rest`. The second `get` pops `alps`, which beats `bradford` on name. Adding `orland 2` sends it straight on to `rest`, and the third `get` pops `bradford`. Then `orlando 3` enters `top` and pushes its worst member, `bradford`, back out to `rest`, so the fourth `get` returns `bradford` again.

## Complexity

- Time: O(log n) per `add` and per `get`: a constant number of heap pushes and pops.
- Space: O(n) for the stored locations.

## Pitfalls

- A new location can outrank ones already returned, so it must pass through `top` first; pushing it straight into `rest` breaks the split.
- Ties are broken by the smaller name, so `"ab"` ranks above `"abc"` and `"a"` above `"b"` when scores match.
- The two heaps use opposite orders; with a single comparator one of them ends up upside down.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `better` | true when the first location ranks above the second |
| `top` | heap of the best `k` locations, worst at the root (`k` = calls to `get` so far) |
| `rest` | heap of all other locations, best at the root |
| `first` | a heap's ordering: should this item sit nearer the root? |
| `location` | the location popped from `rest` on a query |
| `items`, `index`, `parent`, `left`, `right`, `next` | the heap array and positions while sifting |

narration.15: It now belongs to the best k + 1, so move it into top.

narration.33: Take the last item off the array.
narration.35: If the heap is now empty, the root was its only item.
narration.36: Otherwise move the last item to the root and sift it down.
narration.38: Repeat until the item sits above both of its children.
narration.41: Assume the item stays where it is.
narration.42: Prefer the left child if it should come before the item.
narration.43: Prefer the right child if it should come before both.
